title: Moon base: the 354-hour night (second restart: new places and scales)
note: Every sentence comes from the goal's facts in the app (bottlenecks b3.1, b3.3, b2.5 for the temperature shown, and the pending promise 'NASA astronauts would visit the Moon's south pole by 2030'); 'about 14 Earth days' on screen is from b3.1. Every shot is made 3D; nothing real is inserted. Shots: s1x the far side with night sweeping over it (moon_globe.py VIEW 1), s2x Earth turning above the south pole (VIEW 2), s3x the night side in Earth's light (VIEW 4), s4 a person at the habitat (night_video.py SHOT 2), s5x the orbiter (lro_pass.py), s6x the south polar cap with the year strip (VIEW 3), s7 the empty ridge at night (SHOT 6), s8 a person on the ridge summit against Earth through a long lens (SHOT 8).

shots.job: This shot shows night spreading across the Moon from space while the hours count up, so the viewer understands that the whole world goes dark, slowly.
This shot shows Earth turning above the Moon's south pole as the count reaches 354, so the viewer feels one lunar night as two weeks of Earth days.
This shot shows the Moon's night side lit only by Earth while the temperature falls, so the viewer understands what machines there have had to sit out.
This shot shows a person outside the lit habitat in the dark, so the viewer understands what cannot be switched off.
This shot shows the orbiter whose terrain measurements the sunlight study rests on, with the study named, so the viewer knows on what evidence the claim stands.
This shot shows the south polar cap half in night, with one ridge's year of sunlight drawn as a strip, so the viewer sees the dark spells the line speaks of.
This shot shows the ridge empty under the night sky, so the viewer sees that nobody has done it yet.
This shot shows a person standing on that ridge with Earth behind them, so the viewer sees what has been promised.

lines.say: A Moon base would face nights about three hundred and fifty-four hours long.
text: A Moon base would face nights

lines.say: Small landers have survived them by mostly shutting down.
Some ridges at the south pole get sunlight most of the time.
